I think I spent so many years being angry at the older versions of me.

Angry because she trusted too easily.
Angry because she stayed too long.
Angry because she cried over people who did not know how to hold her gently.
Angry because she delayed things.
Angry because she did not become “that woman” as fast as she thought she would.

But lately, I don’t feel like scolding her anymore.

I feel like sitting beside her.

I feel like looking at her with softer eyes and saying,

“I know, sweetheart .
You were doing your best.”

Because now I understand…

She was not weak.
She was tired.

She was not foolish.
She was hopeful.

She was not behind.
She was healing.

She was not wasting time.
She was becoming.

And maybe forgiveness does not always look like one big emotional moment.

Maybe sometimes, it looks like slowly removing the blame from your own heart.

One memory at a time.
One old version at a time.
One heavy “I should have known better” at a time.

I am still learning.

But today, I don’t want to keep punishing myself for surviving in the only ways I knew back then.

I want to love that version too.

Because she carried me here.
And that means something. 🤍

Many of you ask me,
“How do you write?”
“Do you follow a process?”
“How do these stories begin?”

And honestly?

This is how. 🙈🚨

No fancy setup.
No perfect desk.
No fixed writing ritual.

Most of the time, I just pick up my phone, open the Notes app, and start talking.

The phone types.
My mind runs.
My thoughts fall everywhere.

Sometimes it makes sense.
Sometimes it absolutely does not. 😂

The grammar is messy.
The flow is broken.
The sentences are all over the place.
Some lines don’t even know where they are going.

But this is where everything begins.

Before the cute graphics.
Before the polished carousel.
Before the final story that makes you feel something.

There is this.

A messy note.
A random midnight thought.
A voice note I almost forgot.
A sentence that came out of nowhere and said,
“Hey, maybe I can become something.”

I don’t always write beautifully in the beginning.

I just capture what comes.

Then later, I sit with it.
Rewrite it.
Shape it.
Polish it.
Give it heart.
Give it flow.
Give it a little world of its own.

So yes, this is my little messy writing corner.

Read at your own risk. 😂
Nothing is grammatically correct.
Nothing is perfectly structured.
Nothing is aesthetic here.

But it is real.

And I just wanted to share this tiny behind-the-scenes part of my world with you.

Because the final post may look clean…

…but the beginning is usually a chaotic little voice note at midnight. 🥹❤️

You cannot eat soup with a fork.
You will struggle eating noodles with a spoon.

But nobody calls the fork useless.
Nobody calls the spoon unsuccessful.

Because we understand one simple thing:

Different tools have different purposes.

But with humans?

We forget this so quickly.

Someone is amazing at writing.
Someone is amazing at singing.
Someone loves a peaceful 9–5.
Someone feels alive building a business.
Someone grows fast.
Someone grows slowly.
Someone shines in public.
Someone blooms quietly.

And somehow we turn all of this into comparison.

“Am I behind?”
“Am I less talented?”
“Am I failing?”

No, sweetheart.

Maybe you’re not failing.
Maybe you’re just trying to use yourself in the wrong place.
Maybe you’re a fork trying to scoop soup.
Maybe you’re a spoon trying to fight with noodles.

Your purpose is not wrong.
Your pace is not wrong.
Your path is not wrong.

You just need to stop measuring your life with someone else’s design.

Some people are made for stages.
Some are made for pages.
Some are made for boardrooms.
Some are made for classrooms.
Some are made for art.
Some are made for strategy.
Some are made to build slowly, quietly, beautifully.

Different doesn’t mean less.
Different means designed differently.

So before you call yourself behind…
ask yourself:

Am I actually failing?
Or am I trying to scoop soup with a fork?

Save this for the day comparison starts lying to you again.

Self-help books don’t change your life.
You do.

And I think this is where most people get it wrong.

They buy a book expecting it to magically fix their mindset, career, confidence, habits, money, relationships, and entire personality by Sunday evening.

Then when nothing changes, they say,
“Self-help books are useless”.

But maybe the book was never the problem.
Maybe the expectation was.

A book is not here to live your life for you.

It is here to give you direction.
Perspective.

Language for what you’re feeling.

Lessons you didn’t have to learn the hard way.

Mistakes you can avoid before they cost you years.

But after that?

You still have to do the work.
You still have to choose differently.
You still have to apply the lesson when life tests you.

So no, self-help books won’t change your life.

But one line can wake you up.

One idea can shift your thinking.

One page can give you the courage to finally act.
And sometimes, that is enough to start everything.

Read books for guidance.
Not magic.

For perspective.
Not instant transformation.

For speed.
Not shortcuts without effort.

Because books can guide your life.
But only you can change it.

Kindness feels rare today.

Not because people don’t have it anymore.

But because social media has made it so easy to react without feeling the weight of our reaction.

A comment takes 5 seconds to type.
A DM takes 10 seconds to send.
A judgement takes one bad mood.

But the person receiving it?

They may carry it much longer.

And this is not about agreeing with everyone.

You can disagree.
You can have a different opinion.
You can scroll past something that doesn’t match your thoughts.

But somewhere between “having an opinion” and “being cruel”....we need to remember that there is a real human being on the other side.

A person with a life.
A heart.
A story we don’t know.
A day we didn’t see.
A pain they may not be showing.

The internet doesn’t need more people trying to sound smart.

It needs more people who remember how to be human.

Be kind! 🤍

Fiction vs Non-fiction.
The argument that refuses to die.

Some people say fiction is “just stories”.

Some people say non-fiction is “more useful”.

But...

That’s such a small way to look at reading.

Fiction teaches you how people feel.
Non-fiction teaches you how things work.

Fiction gives you empathy.
Non-fiction gives you clarity.

Fiction stretches your inner world.
Non-fiction sharpens your outer world.

One helps you understand humans.
The other helps you understand patterns.

One gives your soul a place to breathe.
The other gives your mind a tool to use.

So no, the smartest readers don’t pick sides.

They read fiction when life feels too dry.
They read non-fiction when life feels too messy.
They know both have a place.

Because sometimes you don’t need a lesson.
You need a story.

And sometimes you don’t need escape.
You need direction.

So who wins?

Neither.

The reader who knows what they need wins.
What do you read more.... fiction or non-fiction?

Some books don’t just tell a story.

They quietly hold up a mirror.

The Alchemist feels simple on the surface.

A boy.
A dream.
A journey.
A treasure.

But the more you sit with it, the more you realise…

This book is not really about finding gold.

It is about becoming the kind of person who is brave enough to follow the whisper.

Because most of us don’t ignore our dreams because we don’t care.

We ignore them because they ask something from us.

Courage.
Trust.
Patience.
Faith.
Movement before certainty.

And that is where the real journey begins.

Not when everything is clear.

But when something inside you keeps saying,
“There is more for you than this”.

Maybe that feeling is not random.

Maybe it is your own life calling you back to yourself.

7 out of 10 people have a mortality problem they are trying to solve with calendars.

More planning.
More hacks.
More routines.
More apps.
More ways to squeeze life into neat little boxes.

But Four Thousand Weeks reminds you of something uncomfortable:

You will never get to everything.

Not because you are lazy.
Not because you are behind.
Not because you are failing.

Because you are human.
And strangely…
that is not depressing.
It is freeing.

Because when time is limited,
everything cannot matter equally.

Every yes becomes sacred.
Every distraction becomes expensive.
Every ordinary day becomes part of your life.

So maybe the goal is not to do more.
Maybe the goal is to stop spending your life on things that don’t deserve your life.

Choose what matters.

Let some things remain unfinished.

Protect your attention.

Because your weeks become your years.
And your years become your life.

Most people don’t have a time problem.
They have a too-many-yeses problem.

Too many commitments.
Too many meetings.
Too many “quick calls”.
Too many things they agreed to because saying no felt uncomfortable.

And then they wonder why life feels heavy.

That’s what Essentialism teaches so beautifully:

Doing less is not laziness.
It is clarity.

Because every yes has a hidden cost.

Your time.
Your energy.
Your attention.
Your peace.
Your better opportunities.

The goal is not to squeeze more into your life.
The goal is to stop giving your life to things that don’t deserve it.

Do less.
But do what matters most.

That is where life becomes lighter.

That is where you finally start feeling like you again.

I was thinking about this today…

We never question nature.

A bamboo takes years.
A mango takes years.
Some plants grow in months.

And we’re okay with that.

We don’t look at a coconut tree and say,
“why are you so slow?”

We don’t compare one tree to another
and decide which one is doing life better.

We understand something very simple:

everything grows in its own time.

But when it comes to us?

Suddenly:
we’re late
we’re behind
we’re not doing enough

We forget the same rule we accept so easily in nature.

Maybe nothing is wrong with you.

Maybe nothing is “late”.

Maybe…

you’re just growing in a way that takes time.

And that’s not a flaw.

That’s your timeline.

When it’s your season,
things will make sense in a way
you can’t force right now.

Till then…

grow quietly. 🌱💙

Most people don’t have a strategy problem.

They have a quitting problem.

And the scary part?
It doesn’t feel like quitting.

It feels like:
“Maybe this isn’t right for me.”
“Maybe I should try something else.”
“Maybe I need a better plan.”

Sounds logical.
Sounds mature.
Sounds smart.

But sometimes…
it’s just a well-dressed excuse to escape discomfort.

——

We’ve been trained to chase clarity.

But clarity doesn’t come first.
Commitment does.

You don’t figure things out
and then go all in.

You go all in…
and then things start making sense.

—

The people you admire?

They didn’t always know what they were doing.
They just refused to walk away early.

That’s it.

No secret formula.
No hidden blueprint.

Just staying when it stopped being exciting.

—

So before you switch paths again…

Ask yourself one uncomfortable question:

“Am I changing direction…
or just avoiding the hard part?”

Be honest.

That answer will save you years.

You know what’s exhausting?

Trying to win at everything.

Trying to look calm.

Look successful.
Look unbothered.
Look “evolved”.

Meanwhile your brain is fighting 47 imaginary battles a day.

Nobody tells us this part!

You’re not tired because life is hard.
You’re tired because you’re emotionally over-invested in things that don’t matter long term.

Random opinions.
Minor criticism.
Looking impressive.
Being right.

That constant mental noise?

It’s optional.

The shift isn’t becoming cold.
It’s becoming selective.

Selective with your energy.
Selective with your outrage.
Selective with your standards.

The older I get, the more I realise:

Peace isn’t found.

It’s chosen.

And sometimes maturity just looks like… shrugging and moving on.

Let me tell you something that hit me like a truck when I first read it.

Every time you open your mouth to convince someone of something, a job interview, a first date, asking for a raise, you have exactly 4 seconds.

Not 4 minutes. 
Not 4 hours. 
4 seconds.

That's how long it takes for a human brain to decide if you're worth listening to. Jordan Belfort calls this the "Straight Line"... the shortest path between "hello stranger" to "yes, I'm in".

Here's the wild part 👇

Every human decision ever made boils down to 3 things:

1. Do I trust you?
2. Do I trust your product/idea?
3. Do I trust the company/situation behind you?

So next time someone says no to you... it's not about your words. It's about which of those 3 they don't believe yet.

You're not losing arguments. You're losing trust.

Now here's how you FIX it 🔧

👉 Fix trust in YOU: Speak with certainty. Slow down. Stop over-explaining. Confident people don't ramble, they declare.

👉 Fix trust in your IDEA: Use a real story. Not stats. Not logic. A story of someone who did it and won. The brain remembers stories, not bullet points.

👉 Fix trust in the SITUATION: Remove the risk for them. "Try it, and if it doesn't work, walk away." People say yes when they feel safe, not when they feel pressured.

The moment all 3 click? That's when people stop saying "let me think about it" and start saying "where do I sign?"

You're not bad at persuasion. You were just never taught the right system.🔥
